parsed_answer.content: Graph theory is the bedrock of complex system modeling, from dependency resolution in build tools like Maven to routing packets in distributed networks. BFS (Breadth-First Search) and DFS (Depth-First Search) are the primary traversal strategies; BFS uses a Queue to explore nodes layer-by-layer, making it ideal for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs, while DFS utilizes a Stack (or recursion) to dive deep into branches, which is essential for pathfinding and backtracking. Cycle detection is a critical invariant check, typically performed via DFS by tracking nodes in the current recursion stack to identify back-edges that signal circular dependencies. Dijkstra's Algorithm extends this by calculating the shortest path in weighted graphs using a PriorityQueue to greedily select the lowest-cost edge, effectively managing the 'relaxation' of node distances. Topological Sort, often implemented via Kahn's Algorithm or DFS post-order traversal, provides a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, u comes before v. This is the exact mechanism used in the 'Course Schedule' problem to determine if a valid sequence of prerequisites exists, effectively detecting cycles in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

items: BFS memory complexity is O(V) as it stores the frontier of the graph, while DFS memory is O(H) where H is the maximum height of the graph, making DFS more space-efficient for deep, sparse trees.
In Dijkstra's algorithm, the use of a PriorityQueue ensures O(E log V) time complexity; failing to use a min-heap results in O(V^2), which is catastrophic for large, dense network graphs.

Cycle detection in directed graphs requires distinguishing between 'visited' nodes and nodes currently in the 'recursion stack'. Marking a node as visited globally is insufficient because it ignores cross-edges that don't form cycles.

Topological Sort is only applicable to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). If the graph contains a cycle, the algorithm will fail to include all nodes in the final ordering, which is the standard way to validate a Course Schedule.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Insight: When implementing Dijkstra, always watch for floating-point precision issues if using weights as doubles, and ensure your graph representation (Adjacency List vs. Matrix) matches your density requirements. A common production trap is using an Adjacency Matrix for sparse graphs, leading to O(V^2) space complexity that triggers OutOfMemoryErrors on large datasets.
